idiom_name: Dictionary<String, Symbol> per scope + parent link
implementation_notes: Swift's standard library supplies Dictionary and Array but no symbol model, so the table is written by hand: a Scope type holding [String: Symbol] and a parent reference, a stack of open scopes pushed on every scope-establishing construct, and define/lookup walking outward. What replaces the classic structure is Dictionary plus value types - entries can be structs, the scope chain can be an array of indices into an arena, and Optional terminates the parent link - while the define/resolve passes remain explicit. Keep the hand-written table for compilers and DSLs; Swift's own front end keeps ASTScope (unqualified and member lookup, sequential and brace scopes, lookups recorded per scope) internal to the compiler, so tooling either reimplements it or uses swift-syntax's public SwiftLexicalLookup library, which is the second variant.
pitfalls: Dictionaries and arrays are value types with copy-on-write: assigning a scope into a stack copies it lazily, so mutating the stack copy after a definition can silently discard bindings - keep scopes in one class or an arena and pass references or indices.

Swift's scoping is sequence-sensitive: brace statements, closures, if/guard bindings and catch clauses have declarative order within one construct (the compiler models them as sequential scopes), so a resolver that only opens a scope per function body resolves names that are not yet visible.

Resolution must be per source file before later phases see it: syntax-based lookup is position-dependent, so cache a binding per identifier occurrence rather than per name to avoid stale answers after edits.

variants.name: swift-syntax SwiftLexicalLookup
variants.implementation_notes: For Swift source, the swift-syntax package ships SwiftLexicalLookup: a stateless, bottom-up unqualified-lookup library whose public entry point is an extension on SyntaxProtocol (lookup(_:with:) taking a LookupConfig) that returns the names an identifier refers to, ordered by visibility - innermost scope first - deliberately mirroring the compiler's internal ASTScope behaviour, including sequential-scope handling via LookupConfig.finishInSequentialScope. What replaces the classic structure is that public lookup API over a parsed source file. The trade-offs are that it resolves Swift syntax rather than your own language, that lookups are computed on demand instead of materialising a reusable table, and that a few ASTScope nuances (for example closure shorthand parameters like $0) remain intentionally different.
pitfalls: The lookup is position-based and stateless: results are only meaningful for the exact syntax node you asked from, so cache per occurrence and re-run after every edit instead of storing results.

LookupConfig changes the answer (finishing in the innermost sequential scope versus continuing outward), so a wrapper that hides the config produces results that disagree with the compiler for code inside nested brace statements.
